paragraphs: The man in the khadi shirt came, held an election for the Federation office-bearers, and made me secretary of the student branch. My friend S. P. Chidambaram was made treasurer. From the day the office-bearers were elected, my mind was in turmoil. My young mind feared: "If this goes on, where will we end up? With the Communists? With the Congress?"

Before long there were signs of growing Congress-Communist dominance within the Federation. That dominance even dared to launch its advance through me. A Congress member of the executive said, "Why don't we adopt 'Long live Tamil! Let Hindi grow!' as the slogan of our Federation?" Students sympathetic to the Communists nodded too. I refused.

I did not sleep all night. Dawn came. I went straight to the house of my friend Chidambaram, the Federation treasurer. He had one hundred rupees in membership fees. I asked him for it at once and got it. "I am going to dissolve our Federation. I am going to return the members' money," I said, and began returning the fees. Only twenty-five rupees was actually returned. The remaining members said, "We do not mind if the Federation is dissolved. Let the fee stay with you."

That very evening an organization called the Tamil Students' Association was formed. I still had seventy-five rupees, didn't I? I enrolled in the new association all those whose fees made up that seventy-five rupees. At the same time we came into contact with the Tamil Nadu Tamil Students' Association started in Salem by a man named Venkataraman, and the Tiruvarur association too came to be called the Tamil Nadu Tamil Students' Association.
I never saw again the comrade who had thought of trapping me in his net. He tried to revive the Federation, failed, and went away.

At the beginning of 1941 the inaugural celebration of the Tamil Nadu Tamil Students' Association was held. We then worked to establish Tamil Nadu Tamil Students' Associations in Thanjavur and other districts. Its annual festival was celebrated with great splendour in Tiruvarur in 1942.

For that festival Bharathidasan composed a song beginning:

"In Tiruvarur, where the cuckoo sings in the cool grove,
behold the Tamil Nadu Tamil Students' Association!"

and ringing out:

"Look—the host of Tamil lions has risen!
See it seek the enemy ranks to tear them apart!"

The annual festival is taking place in Tiruvarur. In Kumbakonam, the Dravidian Students' Association conference organized by Thavamani Rasan and Karunanandam is beginning! Anbazhagan and Mathiazhagan, who took part in that conference, came to Tiruvarur and delivered stirring speeches.

Most of those invited to the festival did not come. I learned this only when I went to the railway station to receive them. I stood there with tears filling my eyes. Fortunately, just then Anbazhagan and Mathiazhagan arrived and consoled me.

Could not those who had agreed to come and then stayed away at least have returned the travel money? They did not. I had no money in hand to send back those who had come, or the others who had suddenly been brought in. Time was running out. My mind was no longer on the festival. I ran to those who had signed pledges for donations; they put me off for a week or ten days. I thought and thought. I saw no way out. Very well, I decided—I would have to steal.

My mother was adamant about one thing: she wanted me to wear a gold chain around my wrist. I was embarrassed to wear it. Even into the fifth or sixth standard, I had gone to high school with my hair braided, but now I felt awkward wearing a chain around my wrist. But Mother wanted the pleasure of seeing it on me, so I wore it for her.

One link had broken, so the chain had been put away in my mother's box until it could be repaired. I remembered that. I entered the house. Mother was busy near the well in the backyard; Father was fast asleep. I crept along the verandah and into the room like a cat and looked for the box.

Alas! Even now I can remember how my heart pounded at that moment. "Steal it?" the question arose. "What else can I do? How am I to send the speakers who have come back to their towns?" came the answer. "What will Mother go through when she finds the gold chain missing? Are we a family wealthy enough to say, 'Never mind, we can make another chain'?" Questions like spears pierced my heart.

I approached the place where the box was kept. What a surprise! The box was open, as though it had been left that way just for me. And there lay the gold chain, curled like a baby snake fresh from the egg. My hand trembled. My throat went dry. My eyes filled. There was no other way. I stole it.

I rushed out, called my friend Thennan, and went to the Chettiar Bank in Tiruvarur. I pledged the chain for fifty rupees and got the money. I sent the speakers back to their towns with ample fare and returned with a deep sigh of relief.

There was uproar at home. Mother spun about here and there like a top. Father poured out his anger: "Why did you leave the box open?" Mother cursed, "Who knows what wretched sinners took it!" I watched the drops falling from her eyes, and I too felt like crying. "They came into my house and stole it! May they turn to dust!" Such words came from Mother's trembling voice.

One thought gave me courage: everyone born into this world is going to turn to dust anyway! Besides, Mother had not fixed a deadline in her curse for when the thief should turn to dust. That gave me some comfort. I joined the others and began searching for the chain. Could something that had to be looked for at the Chettiar Bank be found by searching the corners of the house? We even consulted magic and divination, but nothing helped.

Until we moved from that house two or three years later, searching for the chain became almost a daily task for my mother. Whenever she went to the backyard she would stir through the rubbish heap, or poke into a pit where water had collected. The interest on the chain pledged for fifty rupees mounted until the chain was on the verge of being lost altogether. It was sold, the debt was paid, and with the four or five rupees left over my friends and I ate at a hotel and went to the cinema. That was the end of the chain's story.

Mother would touch my hand again and again and grieve, "My dear boy's wrist is bare!" Many years later, when I told her the truth, she was pleased as well. "You mischievous boy!" she said. The approval in her heart showed on her face, and I understood that too. But could I have told her then? I could not.
Thus once I stole in a way that hurt my mother's heart; and another time, in a way that hurt the heart of my beloved wife.

For a public meeting held on behalf of the Students' Association I had invited Comrade Sanarthanam. He came. I had sent him the fare to come. But how was I to send him back? Those who had asked me to arrange the meeting, and those who had climbed the stage to show off their own importance, had all gone home.

Thinking that I would somehow collect the money and send the comrade back, I asked him to stay one more day. He stayed. By the next evening I had still found no one who would give me money. I went home.

There was a sandal-paste bowl that had been given to my wife as a wedding gift. She kept her turmeric and kumkum in it. I took the bowl, hid it, and slipped out. I begged a relative named Jeyaseelan to take it and borrow ten rupees against it. He tried to stop me. I would not give in; finally he agreed and brought back the money.

The public-meeting problem was settled. Everyone blamed my wife for having lost the sandal-paste bowl. They scolded her. Poor woman—she could do nothing but cry; she could not answer them. I did not reveal the truth. Watching my wife suffer, I would weep inwardly.
